newsitem.title: SINGAPORE: WTO infotech deal seen spurring investment in Asia.
newsitem.headline: WTO infotech deal seen spurring investment in Asia.

text.p: A global deal to scrap tariffs on information technology products will likely spur a shift of investment from Europe to Asia and benefit big corporate players who already dominate key market sectors, analysts say.

The European Union said on Thursday it had agreed with the United States to scrap tariffs on billions of dollars worth of infotech products by 2000, clearing the way for a broader global deal with Japan, Canada and key developing nations.

Trade ministers from the 128-member World Trade Organisation (WTO) have been struggling at their meeting in Singapore this week to clinch a pact to eliminate tariffs on some 180 products in the fast-growing infotech sector, estimated now to be worth some $600 billion annually, by the year 2000.

Negotiators from the Big Four trade partners -- the United States, Japan, the European Union and Canada -- had been at odds over key issues such as product coverage even as they sought to persuade other WTO members including key Asian nations to join in the proposed Information Technology Agreement (ITA).
A senior Japanese trade official said Big Four disputes over product coverage had nearly all been settled, although some gaps still remained between Japan and the EU.

Compromise between the United States and the EU had resulted in a deal covering the bulk of industrial information technology products, as well as digital photocopiers and capacitors -- circuits used in electronic equipment-- while excluding consumer electronics and audio materials. Final agreement depends on countries representing about 90 percent of world trade in the sector joining the pact by March 15, 1997.

U.S. officials have touted the deal as a huge plus for American corporate profits. "The ITA opens up markets that are at the core of U.S. competitiveness, expanding opportunities for America's world-class producers of software and semiconductors, computers and telecommunications equipment," the U.S. Trade Reprentative's office said last month.
Analysts agreed that U.S. firms' lead in key infotech sectors meant that such companies would see big benefits.
"It is only natural that America is keen, given their strong position in personal computers, software and cellular phones," said an analyst at a foreign brokerage in Tokyo.

Japan, whose tariffs on many infotech products are already at or close to zero, has also been keen to see an infotech pact forged. Together, Japan and the United States account for over one-third of global infotech exports.

"The agreement is extremely welcome," said Takeshi Sakurai, a deputy general manager at Japan's Mitsubishi Electric Corp. "Japan already had zero tariffs and now EU and U.S. tariffs will come down, so there will be a level playing field.
Brussels stands to lose most, both in terms of protection for domestic industry and incentives for foreign firms to invest inside Europe so as to get around tariff barriers.
Mitsubishi Electric's Sakurai said that while Europe's lagging microchip sector would suffer, its advanced telecommunications industry, for example, would benefit.
Tariff elimination means multinational firms keen to take advantage of lower Asian labour costs will have good cause to shift investment and output to Asia, some analysts said.
"They will increase investment in Asia, where labour is cheaper, and export to Europe," said David Benda, industry analyst at BZW Securities in Tokyo.

In all, some 30 countries including key players in the dynamic Asia-Pacific markets, are expected to join the infotech pact initially -- although some want flexibility over the timing of the tariff elimination, a Japanese official said.

"Asia will be the fastest-growing market for infotech products," Sakurai said. "And as they build up their telecommunications infrastructure, they will be able to easily use the most advanced technology," he said.
